entries.1:1: God gave Obadiah a message about the nation of Edom, and word was spreading that other nations were getting ready to attack them. It reminds us that God sees and announces what is coming before it happens.
entries.1:2: God says Edom will become small and unimportant, looked down on by others. Pride in their position would not protect them from being humbled.
entries.1:3: Edom felt safe because their cities were built high in rocky cliffs, and their pride convinced them no one could touch them. It warns us that feeling untouchable is a dangerous illusion.
entries.1:4: Even if Edom rose as high as an eagle or built among the stars, God says he would still bring them down. No height or strength can put anyone beyond God's reach.
entries.1:5: Thieves or grape pickers would at least leave something behind, but Edom's ruin would be far more complete. Their loss would be total, not partial.
entries.1:6: God says Edom's hidden treasures and stored wealth would all be searched out and taken. Nothing they had tucked away would escape being found.
entries.1:7: Edom's allies and trusted friends would turn against them and push them out of their own land. People who relied on friendships for safety would find those friends betraying them.
entries.1:8: God says that when that day comes, he will remove Edom's wise men and their wisdom. The cleverness they counted on would not save them.
entries.1:9: Edom's soldiers, especially in Teman, would be terrified, and the whole army would be wiped out. Even brave fighters would lose their courage.
entries.1:10: Edom would be shamed and destroyed because of the violence and cruelty they showed to their brother Jacob, meaning Israel. Treating family or neighbors cruelly brings serious consequences.
entries.1:11: Edom just stood by and watched while foreigners carried off Jerusalem's wealth and cast lots over the city, acting as if they were on the attackers' side. Doing nothing while others suffer makes you complicit.
entries.1:12: God warns Edom not to gloat over Judah's disaster or celebrate when they fell. Enjoying someone else's downfall is wrong in God's eyes.
entries.1:13: Edom should not have entered God's people's city on their day of ruin, enjoyed their trouble, or grabbed their belongings. Taking advantage of someone's worst moment is condemned.
entries.1:14: Edom should not have stood at the crossroads to catch fleeing survivors or hand them over to their enemies. Blocking escape for people in trouble is a serious wrong.
entries.1:15: God's day of judgment is coming for all nations, and each will be treated the way they treated others. What you do to others will come back on you.
entries.1:16: Just as Edom drank and celebrated on God's holy mountain, all the nations will drink the cup of judgment until they are gone. Celebration over others' pain turns into their own downfall.
entries.1:17: But Mount Zion will be a place of safety and holiness, and Jacob's descendants will receive back their inheritance. God promises rescue and restoration for his people.
entries.1:18: Israel and Joseph will burn up Edom like fire burns dry grass, leaving no one in Edom. God's people will prevail, and Edom's line will end, as God has said.
entries.1:19: God's people will take possession of the southern land, the lowlands, Ephraim, and Gilead. The land promised to them will be restored and settled.
entries.1:20: Israelites taken away as prisoners will return and possess land as far as Zarephath, and those exiled from Jerusalem will settle the southern towns. God brings his scattered people home.
entries.1:21: Those saved on Mount Zion will rise up to judge Edom, and in the end the kingdom will belong to the Lord. God's rule wins, and his people share in his victory.
